text: Clicking delete in most applications doesn't mean what people assume. This lesson covers what deletion actually does at three different levels, and where a real right-to-erasure request quietly fails even after the row looks gone.

A soft delete sets a flag, is_deleted true, rather than removing the row, deliberate, it supports undo and audit trails, but the data is still physically present and still sitting in every backup taken before the flag was set. A hard delete actually removes the row. Secure deletion goes further, ensuring the underlying storage is overwritten or the encryption key is destroyed, so it isn't recoverable from disk remnants either.

GDPR Article 17, the right to erasure, gives individuals the right to request deletion under specific conditions, the data's no longer necessary, consent was withdrawn, or it was processed unlawfully. But it's conditional, not absolute. An organization can refuse erasure to comply with a legal retention obligation, to exercise freedom of expression, for public-interest research, or to defend a legal claim. A finance team required to keep an invoice seven years can lawfully decline to erase it early.

Marking a row deleted is the easy ten percent. Backups taken before the deletion still contain the data, and most organizations document that it ages out when the backup's own retention expires instead of editing old backups. Caches and search indexes don't disappear just because the source row did. Logs that captured an email address aren't touched by deleting the account. And downstream processors, an email platform, an analytics vendor, need their own deletion request, the obligation doesn't stop at your own database.
A credible erasure process names all of these locations up front, not one at a time when a request arrives. Next up: data subject requests, the broader process this fits inside.
